547.title: Not one sparrow (Luke 12:1–12)
547.hook: five sparrows sold for two pennies, and none forgotten; your hairs are numbered
547.howItsDone: The hymn His Eye Is on the Sparrow draws on the sparrow sayings in Matthew and Luke, and Francis of Assisi is remembered for preaching to the birds.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a cup clean on the outside, and a God who made the inside too. Your line was the inside too. What quiet, generous thing did you do? Day five hundred forty-seven.

Luke says the crowd had grown past counting, so big that people were treading on one another. And Jesus turns first to his own friends and talks about fear. Not the crowd's fear, theirs. Fear of being found out, fear of powerful people, fear of standing up in front of judges one day and not knowing what to say. It's a heavy start. And then, to make his point, he reaches for something small from the marketplace: sparrows, sold five at a time.

In the King James Bible: "Are not five sparrows sold for two farthings, and not one of them is forgotten before God?" Farthing is the King James word for a small coin; the Greek says assarion. Now set Luke beside Matthew. In Matthew's Gospel, Jesus says two sparrows are sold for one farthing. In Luke, five for two. Some readers do the arithmetic: pay for four, and the seller throws in a fifth for free. A bird not even worth a price. And not one of them, Jesus says, is forgotten before God. Then he comes closer: "But even the very hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not therefore: ye are of more value than many sparrows." Numbered. Not loved in general, as a crowd, but known down to a detail you don't even know about yourself. That's the ground under everything else he says in this passage. Don't fear those who can only kill the body. Say openly who you belong to. And when you're dragged before authorities, don't rehearse a speech, because, as he puts it, "the Holy Ghost shall teach you in the same hour what ye ought to say." In Acts, Luke's second book, Peter and Paul do stand before councils and governors. Courage, in this passage, doesn't come from being tough. It comes from being known: if not one sparrow is forgotten, Jesus tells his friends, they need not fear.
screen: then, large: `NOT ONE OF THEM IS FORGOTTEN BEFORE GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, in two parts. Today, if you can, put out a few crumbs or seeds for the birds, or just stop and watch some, the small ordinary ones nobody photographs. For now, settle and breathe. Think of the thing you're most afraid of this week. Hold it for a moment. Then picture the fifth sparrow, the one thrown in for free, and the line that not one of them is forgotten. If you pray, you can place your fear next to that sparrow. If you don't, simply hold the fear and the sparrow side by side. The bell holds the time.
Assarion, the small Greek coin sparrows were sold for: five birds for two coins, the fifth one thrown in free, and not one of them forgotten before God.
Your line: not one forgotten. Today, notice the person in the room most easily overlooked, and let them know you've seen them. Day five hundred forty-seven.

548.title: Rich toward God (Luke 12:13–21)
548.hook: someone asks him to split an inheritance, and he warns against greed
548.howItsDone: Christians read the rich fool when thinking about money, wills and generosity; some churches teach tithing, giving a set share of income, and some Christians name charities in their wills as a way of being rich toward God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, five sparrows for two coins, the fifth one free, and not one sparrow forgotten. Your line was not one forgotten. Who did you notice? Day five hundred forty-eight.

Jesus has just been talking about courage before judges and the Holy Spirit's help. And a voice from the crowd cuts right across it. "Master, speak to my brother, that he divide the inheritance with me." You can almost hear the family behind it. A parent has died. Someone thinks they got less than their share. There have been arguments at the kitchen table, and maybe nobody's speaking now. So the man brings it to the teacher everyone is listening to. Surely he'll take my side.

The law of Moses had rules for how an inheritance was split. But Jesus won't do it. "Man, who made me a judge or a divider over you?" He doesn't rule on who's right. He goes underneath the question: "Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth." The Greek word for covetousness is pleonexia, the itch for more. Not wanting things, exactly; wanting more than. More than my brother. More than last year. Then he tells a story. A rich man's land produces a huge harvest, and he has a conversation. But listen to who's in it. He thinks within himself. He makes plans: I will pull down my barns, I will build greater. And then he talks to his own soul: "Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry." Nobody else is there. No family, no neighbor, no worker who brought the harvest in, no God. Only him, his barns and his soul. That night, God speaks for the first time in the story and calls him a fool. His life is required of him, and the question is who will own it all now. Then the last line: "So is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God." Rich toward God. Not poor, necessarily. Rich in a direction. Wealth that faces outward, toward God and other people, instead of inward into bigger barns. And notice how it loops back to the brothers. An inheritance fight is exactly what the rich fool's barns could turn into.

Here's the practice: settle one small dispute generously. Settle and breathe. Bring to mind a small disagreement you're carrying: whose turn it is to do the dishes, who owes whom for lunch, a borrowed thing never returned, a sibling squabble about something left behind. Notice the part of you that keeps score. Now imagine letting the score go, giving a little more than your share. What would that cost you, really? Decide on one generous move, and plan to make it today. If you pray, you can ask for a heart that faces outward. The bell holds the time.
Pleonexia, Greek for covetousness, the itch for more: wealth that faces outward, toward God and other people, instead of inward into bigger barns and a conversation with only yourself.
Your line: treasure that faces outward. Today, make your one generous move in that small dispute, and let someone else come out ahead. Day five hundred forty-eight.

549.title: Fear not, little flock (Luke 12:22–34)
549.hook: it's your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom
549.howItsDone: Some Christians return to this passage in times of money worry, and some religious communities, such as Franciscan friars and Poor Clares, give up personal possessions as a discipline of trust.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a man who talked only to his own soul, and a warning to be rich toward God. Your line was treasure that faces outward. Did you make your generous move? Day five hundred forty-nine.

This time the words are for his disciples, Luke says, not the crowd. Fishermen who left their boats. A former tax collector. Women who were supporting the group out of their own means. No house of their own, no regular income, heading toward Jerusalem with a teacher who keeps making powerful people angry. If anyone had a reason to lie awake doing sums, it was this group. And he looks at them, a small band on a dusty road, and calls them by a tender name.
screen: `A SMALL BAND ON A DUSTY ROAD.`

segments.voice: First he points at the sky. "Consider the ravens: for they neither sow nor reap; which neither have storehouse nor barn; and God feedeth them." Matthew just says the birds. Luke names ravens, scavengers, a bird the law of Moses listed as unclean. Even the bird nobody would put on a greeting card is fed. Then the field: "Consider the lilies how they grow: they toil not, they spin not; and yet I say unto you, that Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these." Then he asks a sharp little question: which of you, by worrying, can add one cubit to your height, or a single hour to your life? And then the line Luke saves for last: "Fear not, little flock; for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom." Little flock. Small, vulnerable, the kind of group a wolf would notice. He doesn't pretend they're strong. He says they're loved. And good pleasure is a warm phrase in Greek. It's the same family of word the angels sang at his birth, good will toward men, and the same one the voice used at his baptism: in thee I am well pleased. In Jesus' words, the kingdom isn't handed over reluctantly, after enough worry. It is the Father's delight to give it. Then comes the next instruction: sell what you have, give alms, keep treasure where moths and thieves can't reach. In the passage, the giving follows the not fearing. And then the line that sums up the whole chapter so far: "For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also."

Here's the practice: give one thing away. Settle and breathe. Let one worry about money or the future come up, and name it plainly. Then think of the ravens, fed without a barn, and let the worry sit a little lighter for a moment. Now choose one thing to give away today: a coat you don't wear, a book you've finished, some money to someone who needs it more. Something you'd notice, but not miss terribly. Picture handing it over. If you pray, you can say the line quietly: fed without a barn. The bell holds the time.
Fear not. Jesus' words to a small, vulnerable band of followers: it is your Father's good pleasure, God's delight, to give you the kingdom.
Your line: fed without a barn. Today, give away the thing you chose, and notice whether your heart goes with it. Day five hundred forty-nine.

550.title: Lamps burning (Luke 12:35–59)
550.hook: be like servants waiting up for their master
550.howItsDone: Christians read watching passages like this one especially in Advent, the season of waiting before Christmas, and many churches keep a candle burning or light a new one each week as a sign of readiness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ravens and lilies, and a small band of followers told fear not, little flock. Your line was fed without a barn. What did you give away? Day five hundred fifty.

A big house, late at night. The master has gone to a wedding feast, and in that world a wedding could run for days, so nobody knows when he'll be back. Midnight? Three in the morning? The servants could all go to bed. Or they could do what Jesus describes: keep their robes tucked into their belts, keep the oil lamps trimmed and burning, and listen for a knock. Anyone who has ever waited up for a teenager to come home, or sat by the phone for news from a hospital, knows this kind of night.

In the King James Bible: "Let your loins be girded about, and your lights burning." Girded loins sounds strange now, but it's a picture of readiness. People wore long robes, and to run or work you tucked the hem up into your belt. It's the ancient way of saying roll up your sleeves. Then comes the most surprising sentence in the passage. "Blessed are those servants, whom the lord when he cometh shall find watching: verily I say unto you, that he shall gird himself, and make them to sit down to meat, and will come forth and serve them." Read that again. The master comes home at midnight, finds his servants awake, and instead of being served, he ties on an apron and serves them dinner. Everything upside down. Christians hear in it the same Jesus who, in John's Gospel, washes his friends' feet. What are they waiting for? Most Christians read this as the return of Christ at the end of time, which, Jesus says, comes at an hour when you think not. Many also hear it about every ordinary day: being awake to God, and to people, right now. The chapter then gets more urgent. "For unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required." You can read the sky and know rain is coming, Jesus says, so why can't you read this moment? And if you have a quarrel, settle it on the way, before it reaches the judge. All of it says one thing. Don't sleepwalk. The knock could come in the middle of any conversation.

Here's the practice: stay awake. Settle and breathe, and for these two minutes, be like a servant listening for a knock. Notice every sound: a car, a clock, your own breath. Don't drift. When your mind wanders, bring it back, the way you'd jolt upright if you heard footsteps at the door. Then think ahead to one conversation you'll have today, perhaps one you usually half listen to. Decide to be fully awake in it: phone down, eyes up, really hearing. If you pray, you can ask to be found watching. The bell holds the time.
Lamps burning. Servants waiting up with their robes tucked in and their lights lit, and a master who comes home and serves them.
Your line: keep your lamps lit. Today, in the conversation you chose, stay awake from the first word to the last. Day five hundred fifty.

551.title: One more year (Luke 13:1–9)
551.hook: a barren fig tree gets one more year of digging and manure
551.howItsDone: In the Catholic Sunday readings, Luke 13:1–9 falls in Lent, the season of repentance, and some Christians hear the gardener as Christ pleading for time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, servants waiting up with lamps burning, and a master who served them dinner. Your line was keep your lamps lit. Were you awake in that conversation? Day five hundred fifty-one.

The news comes first. Some people come to Jesus with a terrible story: Pilate, the Roman governor, has killed Galileans while they were offering sacrifices. And Jesus adds another disaster. A tower at Siloam, in Jerusalem, collapsed and killed eighteen people. When disaster strikes, someone says it out loud, or thinks it quietly: they must have done something. Jesus asks the question directly, and answers it. Were they worse than everyone else? "I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish." Then, instead of explaining suffering, he tells a story about a tree.

A man has a fig tree planted in his vineyard. Three years running he comes looking for fruit, and finds none. So he tells the gardener, in the King James Bible: "cut it down; why cumbereth it the ground?" Why let it take up space? It's a fair question. The tree has taken up ground for three years and given nothing back. But the gardener answers: "Lord, let it alone this year also, till I shall dig about it, and dung it." Dung it. Manure. The gardener doesn't just ask for more time. He offers to get his hands dirty: loosen the hard ground round the roots, and feed it with the least glamorous stuff on the farm. Here's a small thing in the Greek worth knowing. The gardener's let it alone is a form of aphiēmi, the ordinary verb for let go, leave be. It's also the word the Gospels use for forgive, as in forgive us our sins. So the gardener's request sounds, to a Greek ear, a little like a plea for mercy. Some Christian readers hear Jesus himself in the gardener, pleading for time and doing the digging. And then the story stops. The gardener says, if it bears fruit, well; if not, cut it down after that. We never find out what happened next year. Luke leaves the ending open, the way a life is open. It's a story about urgency, the year is real and it ends, and about patience, the kind that works the soil instead of just waiting. Those two belong together. Disaster doesn't prove anyone deserved it; and the year the gardener asks for is a year of digging.
screen: then, large: `LET IT ALONE THIS YEAR ALSO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give someone one more chance. Settle and breathe. Think of someone you've been close to writing off: a colleague who never delivers, a relative who keeps letting you down. Or maybe it's you. Picture them as that fig tree, and picture yourself as the gardener, asking for one more season. Then ask: what would digging around the roots look like? A real conversation, some help, a little patience with a deadline. Choose one small piece of that work. If you pray, you can ask for the gardener's patience. The bell holds the time.
Aphiēmi, the Greek verb for let it alone, leave be — the gardener's plea for a fruitless fig tree he offers to dig and feed, while the story never tells us how it turned out.
Your line: leave it one more year. Today, do one bit of digging for the person you chose, instead of just waiting for them to change. Day five hundred fifty-one.

552.title: The bent-over woman (Luke 13:10–17)
552.hook: eighteen years stooped; he calls her a daughter of Abraham and she stands up straight
552.howItsDone: Some churches pray for the sick with the laying on of hands, as Jesus does here, and Catholic and Orthodox Christians also anoint the sick with oil.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a fig tree with no fruit and a gardener asking for one more year, aphiēmi. Your line was leave it one more year. What digging did you do for someone? Day five hundred fifty-two.

Eighteen years. That is how long, Luke says, this woman has been bent over, looking at the ground. Feet, dust, the hems of other people's clothes. She can't look up to see a face or the sky. Luke, who tradition says was a physician, describes her carefully: she "was bowed together, and could in no wise lift up herself." And on a Sabbath, she does what she has probably done for years. She comes to the synagogue. Nobody says she asked for anything. Jesus is teaching, and he sees her.

He calls her over and says, in the King James Bible: "Woman, thou art loosed from thine infirmity." He lays his hands on her, "and immediately she was made straight, and glorified God." After eighteen years, perhaps the first thing she sees, looking up, is his face. Then comes an objection, and it's worth hearing fairly. The leader of the synagogue is indignant and says to the crowd: "There are six days in which men ought to work: in them therefore come and be healed, and not on the sabbath day." He's protecting something precious, the Sabbath rest that God commanded. He isn't against healing; he's against doing it today. Jesus answers with an argument the leader himself would recognize, from the lesser to the greater. On the Sabbath, every one of you unties your ox or donkey and leads it to water. Untie. Then: "And ought not this woman, being a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan hath bound, lo, these eighteen years, be loosed from this bond on the sabbath day?" Listen to the words: untie the animal, she was bound, she should be loosed. In Luke's Greek, untie and loose are the same verb, and bound is its opposite. If an animal can be untied for a drink, how much more a woman bound for eighteen years? And notice the title. Daughter of Abraham. For eighteen years she had been the bent woman, a body people stepped around. He gives her a family name, a place in Israel's story. Luke says all the people rejoiced. The Sabbath, a day of freedom, became the day she was set free.
screen: then, large: `SHE WAS MADE STRAIGHT, AND GLORIFIED GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: straighten your back and stand tall. If you can, stand up. If not, sit forward. Let your head drop toward your chest for a moment, and notice how small the world gets: just your knees, the floor. Then, slowly, one bone at a time, roll upward, until your head rises and your eyes find the room. Feel your full height. Breathe there. Think of whatever has kept you bent lately, a weight or a worry or someone's words. If you pray, you can hear the words thou art loosed. If you don't, simply stand in your own height. The bell holds the time.
The bent-over woman. Bound for eighteen years, loosed on a Sabbath, and named a daughter of Abraham as she stood up straight.
Your line: daughter, you are loosed. Today, notice someone others step around, and call them by name. Day five hundred fifty-two.

553.title: Like a mother hen (Luke 13:18–35)
553.hook: how often I would have gathered you, as a hen gathers her chicks
553.howItsDone: Some churches read Jesus' lament over Jerusalem in Lent, and on the Mount of Olives, the chapel of Dominus Flevit has a mosaic of a hen gathering her chicks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bent-over woman, stooped for eighteen years, stood up straight and was called a daughter of Abraham. Your line was daughter, you are loosed. Who did you call by name? Day five hundred fifty-three.

A warning arrives on the road. Some Pharisees come to Jesus, and, it seems, they're trying to help: "Get thee out, and depart hence: for Herod will kill thee." Herod, the ruler of Galilee, the man who, Luke has already told us, beheaded John the Baptist. This is a real threat. And Jesus sends back a message with a bite in it: "Go ye, and tell that fox" that I'm busy healing today and tomorrow, and on the third day I'll finish. So, a fox. Hold onto that animal. Because a few sentences later, Jesus picks an animal for himself.

He doesn't choose a lion, or an eagle. He looks toward Jerusalem, the city where he knows he's heading, and says, in the King James Bible: "O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which killest the prophets, and stonest them that are sent unto thee; how often would I have gathered thy children together, as a hen doth gather her brood under her wings, and ye would not!" A hen. An ordinary farmyard bird. When danger comes, a hawk overhead, a fox at the fence, she can't fight it off. What she can do is spread her wings, call her chicks, and put her own body between them and harm. So here's the picture: Herod the fox, and Jesus the mother hen. One hunts. The other covers, even at a cost. The image wasn't new. Israel's psalms had long pictured God's protection as wings. Psalm 91: "He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust." Jesus takes that old picture and makes it a mother's. And the lament is full of grief, not anger: how often I would have, and you would not. Love that can be refused. The rest of this passage has the same open arms. People will come from east and west, north and south, and sit down in the kingdom of God; and some who are last will be first. Then look at the week behind us. A sparrow not forgotten. A barn too big. A little flock. Lamps burning. A tree given one more year. A bent woman standing straight. And now a hen with her wings open, over a city that might not come.
screen: then, large: `AS A HEN DOTH GATHER HER BROOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: gather your people. Settle and breathe. Bring to mind the people you'd want under your wings: family, friends, the ones who've drifted, perhaps someone who has refused you. See their faces one at a time. Now imagine them around a table, your table, with food and enough chairs. Who's missing? Who would be hard to invite? Choose one evening soon and one or two people to gather, even if it's only soup. If you pray, you can hold each of them under those wings in your mind. The bell holds the time.
Like a mother hen. Jesus pictures himself gathering Jerusalem's children under his wings, a mother's love that covers and can still be refused.
Your line: under her wings. Today, reach out to one person who has drifted, and let them know there is still room. Day five hundred fifty-three, and another week on the path.

fork.setup: friends warn Jesus: Herod wants to kill you, leave now. what does he do?
options: he slips away to the desert.
he sends word to that fox: I'm healing today and tomorrow, and I'm going to Jerusalem.
he asks for a guard.
fork.reveal: "go ye, and tell that fox." he keeps healing, keeps walking toward Jerusalem, and then laments over it like a mother hen.

original.note: Greek: a bird, and especially a hen. the word Jesus chooses for himself over Jerusalem.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gentle picture of Jesus being kind.
what it means: a lament full of grief: love that covers at a cost and can still be refused.
what a scholar hears: Herod the fox and Jesus the hen sit a few verses apart, and the wings echo the psalms' picture of God's shelter.
